reconcile.connective: The strongest defense argues the Hebrew of Genesis 1 never actually names a material for the birds, so the apparent water-versus-ground conflict rests on a mistranslation.

discrepancy.connective: Source critic Richard Elliott Friedman reads Genesis 2 (J) as a separate account in which God hand-forms the animals from the ground, a different picture from Genesis 1 (P), where they are brought forth from the waters.

skeptic.name: Richard Elliott Friedman
skeptic.attribution: Richard Elliott Friedman, Who Wrote the Bible? (1987)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Earlier translators, on the contrary, have rendered the latter as a relative clause, after the πετεινὰ πετόμενα of the lxx, "and with birds that fly;" thus making the birds to spring out of the water, in opposition to Gen 2:19. Even with regard to the element out of which the water animals were created the text is silent …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly engages the water-vs-ground tension by name ("in opposition to Gen 2:19") and harmonizes it: the Hebrew text is silent on the element birds/water-animals were made from, so the conflict dissolves as a translation artifact.

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament (1861-75), on Genesis 1:20
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: Treats this passage directly, arguing the Hebrew of Gen 1:20 is silent on the element animals were formed from and that the water-origin rendering is an erroneous translation that needlessly conflicts with Gen 2:19.
